title: Wisdom's children (Luke 7:18–35)
hook: John had doubts in prison; Jesus answers with what's happening
carry: go and tell what you've seen

segments.voice: Yesterday, the widow of Nain and two crowds meeting at a gate. Your line was he had compassion on her. Whose quiet sadness did you notice? Day five hundred twenty-eight.

John the Baptist is locked up. Luke told us earlier that Herod had shut him in prison, for criticizing the ruler's marriage. The man who lived in open desert air now sits in a cell. And his followers visit and bring him news: healings, crowds, a widow's son raised. News like that might encourage him. Instead John sends two of his disciples to Jesus with a question that sounds like doubt: "Art thou he that should come? or look we for another?" This is the man who baptized Jesus. Who said he wasn't worthy to untie his sandals. Even John, it seems, can wonder in the dark whether he got it right.

Jesus doesn't scold John for asking. He doesn't even answer yes. Luke says that in that same hour he healed many people, and then he told John's messengers: "Go your way, and tell John what things ye have seen and heard; how that the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, to the poor the gospel is preached." It's not an argument. It's a report. Look at what's happening, and let John decide. And the list echoes the scroll of Isaiah that Jesus read in Nazareth: sight to the blind, good news to the poor. Jesus answers in Isaiah's language and lets John draw the line himself. Then a gentle line: "And blessed is he, whosoever shall not be offended in me." Behind offended is the Greek skandalizo, to trip someone up; its noun, skandalon, is a snare or a stumbling block. Blessed is anyone who doesn't trip over me, who doesn't let a Messiah different from what they expected become the thing they stumble on. And as soon as the messengers leave, Jesus praises John to the crowd: "Among those that are born of women there is not a greater prophet than John the Baptist." John's question hasn't lowered him in Jesus' eyes. Then Jesus turns to the crowd with a picture of children in the marketplace, complaining: we played the flute and you didn't dance; we sang a sad song and you didn't cry. John came fasting, and some said he had a devil. Jesus came eating and drinking, and some called him a glutton. Nothing satisfies the critics. "But wisdom is justified of all her children." Wisdom is proved right by what she produces, by the lives that come out of her.
screen: `BLESSED IS HE NOT OFFENDED IN ME.`
`WE PIPED AND YE DID NOT DANCE.`
then, large: `WISDOM IS JUSTIFIED OF ALL HER CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask your doubt out loud. Settle, and breathe. Some questions are hard to say out loud. About faith, about a relationship, about a path already chosen. If you have one, let it come up now. Don't answer it. Just name it, the way John did, clearly, in a sentence. Art thou he? Is this right? Now notice that in the story, asking didn't make John smaller. Right after, Jesus said no prophet was greater. Then, instead of an argument, think about evidence: what have you actually seen and heard lately that speaks to your question, either way? If you pray, you can ask your question to God plainly. If you don't, simply hold it with honesty. The bell holds the time.
Wisdom's children. John asks from prison whether Jesus is the one, and Jesus answers with what's happening, and says wisdom is proved right by her children.
Your line: go and tell what you've seen. Today, ask your question out loud to someone you trust, and tell them, plainly, one thing you've seen that speaks to it. Day five hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Some churches read Matthew's telling of John's question from prison during Advent, and some Christians take comfort that even John the Baptist sent his doubt to Jesus as a question.

fork.setup: John sends messengers asking: are you the one, or should we look for someone else? how do you answer?
options: yes, of course. tell him to stop doubting.
go and tell John what you've seen and heard.
say nothing; he should already know.
fork.reveal: Jesus answers with evidence, the blind seeing and the poor hearing good news, and lets John decide. then he tells the crowd no prophet is greater than John.

original.note: Greek: a snare, a trap's trigger, a stumbling block. behind "offended" in Luke 7:23.

trapdoor: what you thought: John lost his faith in prison.
what it means: John asks honestly, Jesus answers with what's happening, and right after says no prophet is greater.
what a scholar hears: "offended in me" is skandalizo, to trip over something; the blessing is for those who don't stumble over a Messiah they didn't expect.

notes: Luke 7:18–19 does not say John is in prison; that comes from Luke 3:19–20 (and Matthew 11:2). The script cites 3:20.
Herod imprisoned John for rebuking him over Herodias (Luke 3:19); summarized as 'criticizing the ruler's marriage'.
Whether John's question is real doubt or meant for his disciples has been read both ways; the script says 'sounds like doubt' and 'it seems'.
skandalon as a snare or stumbling block: standard lexicon.

Editor review (2026-10-01): fixed 'some called him mad' (Luke 7:33: 'he hath a devil'); 'the greatest of the prophets' (three places) changed to Luke's own wording, no prophet greater; cut the speculation that John 'knew those prophecies'; 'everybody carries a question' no longer tells the listener what they carry; Advent reading attributed to Matthew's version.
